question: A designer offers to let you “shadow me for a day”. What is she inviting you to do?
choices: Watch her at work to learn about the role.
Stand in for her while she takes a day off.
Work with her on a design of your own.
Give her feedback on how she works.
note: Shadowing lets you see a job from the inside. “Stand in for me” would mean doing the job in her place.

question: A graduate likes a job because there’s “room to grow”. What appeals to her?
choices: She could take on more responsibility over time.
She could choose how many hours to work.
She could move to a larger office soon.
She could start without any training.
note: “Room to grow” means there’s scope to develop. Choosing your hours is usually described as “flexible working”.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: “A long commute would be a deal-breaker for me.” What does the speaker mean?
choices: The journey alone could make them turn the job down.
They would ask for travel expenses first.
They would miss the commute from their last job.
The journey is worth discussing after they’ve accepted.
note: A deal-breaker rules an offer out. “I’d want to discuss travel expenses” leaves the decision open.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: An engineering trainee says, “I’d like more hands-on experience.” What is he asking for?
choices: A chance to work with the equipment himself.
A more detailed explanation from the trainer.
An introduction to the people who design it.
More time to read how the equipment works.
note: Hands-on experience comes from doing the work. Reading a manual would build background knowledge.

picture.alt: An old engine with a flywheel.

question: Two placements sound interesting. “I’m keeping my options open,” says Ada. What has she decided?
choices: She wants to consider both before committing.
She has agreed to take both placements.
She’ll take whichever company calls first.
She’s waiting for a better offer elsewhere.
note: Keeping your options open delays a commitment. “I’ll take the first one that calls” gives you a rule for choosing.

picture.alt: A travel suitcase with a blank tag.

question: An interviewer asks, “How do you handle surprises?” You once found a new room when a student play lost its venue. What do you say?
choices: Our venue cancelled on the day, so I moved the play to a classroom.
I’d probably try to find a room if anything like that happened.
I like to know about any changes well before a show starts.
Our drama group had a wonderful audience for our last performance.
note: The venue story shows what you actually did. “I’d probably…” could answer a question about an imagined situation.

picture.alt: An empty stage framed by red curtains.

question: A gallery offers you a placement. You’d love to accept. The advert says Monday to Friday, and you have a compulsory Friday lab. What do you say?
choices: I’m keen. Could I do four days a week until my lab course ends?
Thanks for the offer. I’ll send my details and see you on Monday.
Friday is the only difficult day, so I’ll probably manage somehow.
Thanks for thinking of me. Please offer the place to someone else.
note: The question checks a condition before you commit. “Please offer the place to someone else” fits if you’ve decided to decline.

picture.alt: A clock beside a blank calendar.

question: “Have you ever trained anyone?” You’ve never held a teaching job, but you showed new kitchen staff how to close up safely. How do you answer?
choices: At the café I showed new starters the closing routine and watched them try it.
I’ve never been a teacher. I imagine I’d need some practice first.
I was trained by the café manager when I first started there.
Closing time was my favourite shift because the café was usually quiet and empty.
note: Showing new staff a routine counts as training. “I was trained…” describes what you learned from someone else.

picture.alt: A cooking pot and wooden spoon.

question: A careers adviser asks what matters most to you. Two jobs pay the same. One has regular hours, which you need to finish your degree. What do you say?
choices: Regular hours would matter most while I’m finishing my degree.
Salary would probably settle it if one company paid a little more.
I’d like to know which job comes with more training opportunities.
Both roles sound interesting. I might apply for something similar later.
note: Regular hours explain your priority in this particular choice. “More training opportunities” would fit if learning at work came first.

question: At an interview you hear, “You’d be supporting our editors.” You’re unsure what you’d actually do in a typical week. What do you ask?
choices: Could you walk me through a recent task someone in this role handled?
How many editors have worked their way up from this role?
Would I be joining the editorial team at the same time as anyone else?
How long do most people stay before moving to another team?
note: A recent task makes “supporting” concrete. “Worked their way up” asks about promotion, a useful question later.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: Two placements appeal to your friend. One pays well, the other lets her photograph concerts. She asks which to choose. You don’t know her priorities. What do you say?
choices: What would be harder to give up this term, the income or the photography?
I’d take the concert work. We can sort out the money once you start.
The paid job is the sensible choice. You can always take photos later.
Why don’t we ask the photography placement if it could pay you something?
note: Asking what she’d give up helps her weigh the trade-off. “I’d take the concert work” makes more sense if she asks for your personal preference.

picture.alt: A camera beside a blank photograph.

question: “Could you edit our podcast?” You’ve cut interviews for class but never mixed sound. The producer needs to know what you can handle alone. What do you say?
choices: I can edit the interviews myself. I’d need help with the sound mix.
I’ve worked on audio before, so leave the whole thing with me.
I’ve never mixed sound, so you should probably find another editor.
If someone explains the project, I’m happy to listen to the interviews.
note: The reply draws a clear line between two tasks. “Find another editor” might fit if mixing sound were the whole job.

picture.alt: A laptop with a blank screen.

question: Your application was unsuccessful. You’d like to try again next year and genuinely want one useful piece of feedback. What do you write?
choices: Thanks for letting me know. What could I strengthen before reapplying?
Could you explain how the successful applicants were better qualified than me?
Please reconsider my application. I’m willing to start at short notice.
Thanks for the update. Can you put my name down for next year now?
note: Asking about your own application gives the reader a manageable question. “Please reconsider” would ask them to change the decision.

question: An adviser says, “So you’d prefer to work alone.” You like designing by yourself, but you enjoy discussing drafts with others. What do you say?
choices: For the first sketch, yes. Once I have a draft, I like working with others.
Would it help if I showed you a design I made completely by myself last term?
Could we ask the team how they normally share the work?
Actually, I’d rather talk about the salary and hours first.
note: “For the first sketch” keeps the part that fits and corrects the rest. Showing a solo design could illustrate one part of your work, but it would leave your enjoyment of teamwork unclear.

question: A studio turns down your request for a month-long placement but offers a visit on Tuesday. You’re free and would like to go. What do you write?
choices: Tuesday would be great. What time should I arrive for the visit?
Thank you. Could we discuss a month-long placement during the visit?
Thank you for the update. Let me know if a longer placement comes up.
Could you explain why you can’t offer me the full month after all?
note: The reply accepts the visit and moves the arrangement forward. “Let me know if a longer placement comes up” would suit someone who wanted to wait.

picture.alt: A sealed envelope with a postage stamp.
